prompt: Some people think students should be allowed to use calculators in all math classes. Write an essay arguing for or against this.
text:
# Calculators Belong in Some Math Classes, Not All

Calculators are useful tools, and students should learn to use them well. But allowing them in every math class, at every level, would hurt the learning that math classes exist to provide. Students should use calculators when the lesson is about something other than arithmetic, and put them away when the lesson is building basic skills.

The strongest argument for unrestricted calculators is that they save time. Nobody in a modern job multiplies 4,863 by 27 by hand. A calculator does it faster and with fewer errors, and it frees students to work on harder problems. In a statistics course or a physics-based calculus class, doing long computations by hand would bury the real lesson under busywork. In those classes, calculators should be welcome.

The trouble is that early math classes teach more than answers. When a child works out 7 × 8 or splits 3/4 into parts, they build a sense of how numbers behave. That sense lets them notice when something is wrong. A student who has never developed it will accept any result the screen shows, even if they typed a wrong key and the answer is off by a factor of ten. Number sense is what lets a person judge whether a result is reasonable, and a calculator can't supply it.

Basic skills also support later learning. Algebra depends on fluent arithmetic, and students who count on a calculator for every fraction or negative number tend to struggle when they have to simplify expressions with variables. Their working memory is spent on small steps that should be automatic. Teachers see this often: the student who can't do 12 ÷ 4 without a device finds factoring painfully slow.

There is also a fairness concern. A rule that allows calculators everywhere makes it hard to tell what a test measures. If a question asks students to add fractions and every student has a calculator that does it, the question no longer shows who understands fractions. Teachers need to be able to set the tool aside to find out what students actually know.

A sensible policy is simple. In elementary and middle school, and in the early units of any course where arithmetic or algebraic manipulation is the goal, students should work without calculators. Once those skills are secure, calculators should be allowed, and even required, for tasks like graphing, regression and large data sets. Teachers should also teach how to use them: how to check an answer by estimating, and when a result looks wrong.

Calculators are a good tool, but a tool is only useful to someone who knows what job it is doing. Schools should let students use calculators when understanding is already in place, and hold them back when the calculator would do the learning for the student.
